title: The Borrowed Cipher
premise: Retired detective Coral Okonkwo, who spent years quietly solving deaths the police dismissed as accidents, receives two letters in the same week: one from someone confessing to the fourth death he never solved, and one promising a fifth unless he stops digging. As Coral follows the confession's thread back thirty years to a drowned witness and a corrupt inquest, he realizes the letters come from two different hands—one from the true killer seeking absolution, one from a protégé who learned his methods and wants to erase him. The killer is the town's beloved coroner, whose alibi rests on a death certificate Coral himself once trusted. In the end Coral must choose between exposing the coroner and destroying the only family he has left, and he chooses justice, publishing the truth in the only place no one can suppress it: the front table of his own bookshop.
about_author: Rafael Brightwater is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper editor who covered two decades of unsolved deaths before turning to fiction. He writes mysteries from a converted ferry cabin on the Atlantic coast, where the tide dictates his working hours.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Coral Okonkwo's POV. In his failing bookshop, Coral catalogs stock he can't sell and quietly rereads notes from three 'accidents' he solved off the books. Emotional beat: the ache of a man whose sharpest years are behind him, keeping vigil over truths no one asked for.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Handwriting
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Twin letters arrive: one confessing to the 1994 drowning of Ada Merrick, one promising 'the next one soon.' The handwriting is identical, which should be impossible. Emotional beat: the old thrill of the hunt waking in him like a muscle remembering.

chapters.title: What the Police Called Weather
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, flashback woven in. He revisits the Merrick inquest file at the county archive and finds his own younger signature as a corroborating witness. Emotional beat: dread—the case he never cracked may be the one he helped bury.

chapters.title: The Bookshop at Closing Time
chapters.summary: Deputy Imani Voss's POV. Voss, who suspects Coral's quiet successes, visits the shop under pretense of buying a novel. They circle each other politely. Emotional beat: mutual recognition between two people who both know the law has limits.

chapters.title: Ada Merrick, Restless
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. He interviews Ada's estranged daughter, who reveals her mother had been about to testify against the coroner's office. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into purpose; Coral stops being curious and starts being committed.

chapters.title: The Confession's Grammar
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Close reading of the confession letter reveals details only the killer would know—and one detail that's wrong, deliberately. Emotional beat: the cold realization that the letter is bait, written by someone who studied him.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Alternating Coral and Voss POVs. Coral reconstructs the night Ada died; Voss pulls the old file and finds it was signed off by the same coroner, Dr. Edwin Lark. Emotional beat: two investigations converging without either party admitting it.

chapters.title: The Man Who Buried Everyone
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral attends Lark's retirement dinner, watching the town toast its gentlest public servant. Emotional beat: the vertigo of suspecting someone the whole community loves—and half wanting to be wrong.

chapters.title: A Fifth Letter
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A third letter arrives, not to Coral but to the bookshop's bulletin board: a threat against 'the next witness,' dated for the coming week. Emotional beat: urgency; the game has moved from past to present tense.

chapters.title: The Protégé
chapters.summary: New POV: Martin Hale, a former police archivist, alone in a rented room, writing letters. He believes he is Coral's heir, finishing the work Coral abandoned. Emotional beat: unsettling sympathy for a man whose devotion has curdled into obsession.

chapters.title: Voss Asks the Wrong Question
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss confronts Coral about the Merrick case; he deflects, but she leaves him a copy of the inquest file anyway. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance forming—truth is the one thing they can't afford to withhold from each other.

chapters.title: The Drowned Testimony
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. In a flooded basement records room, Coral finds Ada's never-filed deposition naming Lark. Emotional beat: triumph curdling into horror—proof existed all along, and someone chose the water over the truth.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Lark visits the bookshop, and the two old men speak in pleasantries loaded like pistols. Emotional beat: the terrible intimacy of two people who each know what the other knows.

chapters.title: Hale Makes His Move
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Hale stages an 'accident' targeting the inquest's last living clerk, believing he's protecting Coral's legacy. Emotional beat: dread—the confessor and the killer are not the same person, and both are closing in.

chapters.title: The Clerk Who Lived
chapters.summary: Coral and Voss POVs. The clerk survives, half-drowned, and identifies not Lark but a younger man with careful handwriting. Emotional beat: the case splits open; Coral must now hunt his own shadow.

chapters.title: Reading the Heir
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral traces Hale through borrowed library books and marginalia—his own methods, turned back on him like a mirror. Emotional beat: the shame of a teacher seeing his lessons weaponized.

chapters.title: Lark's Ledger
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss obtains Lark's private death ledgers and finds thirty years of 'accidents' signed with a flourish. Emotional beat: cold fury; the corruption is not one death but a system wearing a kind face.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Lark offers Coral silence, a pension for the bookshop, and the erased file on Coral's own brother's death. Emotional beat: the book's moral crux—justice outside the law, priced in the currency of personal grief.

chapters.title: What Coral Chose Thirty Years Ago
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, extended flashback. We learn Coral once buried evidence to protect his brother, and Lark covered it—binding them ever since. Emotional beat: the theme crystallizes; identity is what we do with our worst choice.

chapters.title: The Tide House
chapters.summary: Coral and Hale POVs. Hale lures Coral to the abandoned tide house where Ada died, intending a final 'collaboration.' Lark arrives to silence them both. Emotional beat: rising terror as three obsessions collide in rising water.

chapters.title: The Verdict of Water
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Voss arrives; Hale, choosing at last to be a witness rather than an heir, gives his letters as evidence before the tide takes the tide house's secrets. Lark is arrested on thirty years of ledgers. Emotional beat: catharsis bought at real cost—Hale goes into custody too, and Coral lets him.

chapters.title: The Front Table
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, epilogue weeks later. Coral publishes the full truth as a slim self-published volume displayed on the shop's front table; Voss buys the first copy, and the town reads what it spent thirty years not seeing. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace—justice delivered not by the law, but by a bookseller who refused to stay invisible.
